author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Option Volatility and Pricing: Book Structure Overview
body: Natenberg's comprehensive practitioner text covers: (Ch.1-3) financial contracts, forward/futures pricing, contract specifications; (Ch.4) expiration P&L and parity graphs; (Ch.5) theoretical pricing models and the Black-Scholes model; (Ch.6) volatility — random walks, normal distributions, standard deviation, scaling; (Ch.7-9) dynamic hedging, Greeks introduction; (Ch.10-13) delta, gamma, theta, vega, rho in detail and across market conditions; (Ch.14-17) introduction to spreads, volatility spreads, calendar and diagonal spreads, synthetics; (Ch.18-19) Black-Scholes and binomial models in depth; (Ch.20-25) vol estimation, trading, and risk management. The defining characteristic: every topic is approached from a probability and risk-management perspective, not from a directional trading perspective.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Short Selling in Derivatives: Sell First, Buy Later
body: In conventional markets, selling requires prior ownership. Derivatives markets invert this: you can sell first and buy back later (short selling). The profit is identical regardless of order — only entry and exit prices matter. This ability to initiate a short position without prior ownership is foundational to: (1) options and futures trading; (2) arbitrage (conversions, reversals); (3) delta-neutral hedging; (4) spread strategies where one leg is short. Market makers depend on the ability to short options freely — they are frequently short the options they sell to customers.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Notional Value of Derivative Contracts
body: A derivative contract has no immediate cash exchange but carries a notional (nominal) value representing the total underlying exposure. For physical commodities: notional = quantity × unit price (e.g., 1,000 units × $75 = $75,000 notional). For cash-settled contracts (stock index futures), physical delivery is impractical — settlement occurs in cash. Notional value matters for: (1) margin requirement calculations (margin is a fraction of notional); (2) understanding true capital at risk vs. initial margin; (3) position sizing relative to portfolio value. A $10,000 margin deposit on a $100,000 notional contract provides 10x leverage.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Futures Margining: Daily Mark-to-Market Settlement
body: Futures contracts require a margin deposit from both buyer and seller as a performance bond. Unlike stock margin (a loan), futures margin is collateral against default. Daily mark-to-market: each day, gains are credited and losses are debited to accounts. If losses reduce the account below the maintenance margin, a margin call is issued. This daily settlement is why futures positions can be held with relatively small capital vs. notional: losses are paid continuously rather than accumulating. Importantly, the daily settlement also means that futures options have 'futures-type settlement' — gains/losses on futures options are credited/debited daily.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Implied Values: Back-Solving for the Unknown Variable
body: Given a pricing model and all inputs except one, the unknown can be back-solved from a market price. This applies to: implied spot price (from forward price), implied interest rate, implied dividend D = [S × (1 + r × t)] − F, and most importantly, implied volatility (from an observed option price). If a contract is fairly priced, its implied value represents the market's consensus estimate of the missing input. Implied volatility is the most critical application — given a market option price and all other known inputs, back-solve the Black-Scholes model to find IV. IV is not calculated directly; it is always inferred.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Dividend Modeling in Option Pricing
body: Equity option pricing requires accurate dividend forecasts. The ex-dividend date (when the stock drops by approximately the dividend amount) reduces the forward price, lowering call values and raising put values. Key inputs: ex-dividend date and dividend amount. Common approach: if a company has paid $0.25 quarterly for 10 quarters, assume $0.25 per quarter going forward. The present value of expected dividends is subtracted from the spot price to compute the forward price. Mispricing dividends systematically biases call values (too high) and put values (too low) for ITM options where dividend impact is significant.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Moneyness: At-the-Money, In-the-Money, Out-of-the-Money
body: Precise definition: ATM requires exercise price exactly equal to current underlying price. In practice (exchange-traded options): ATM = the call and put whose exercise price is closest to current price. ITM call: exercise price < current price. OTM call: exercise price > current price. ITM put: exercise price > current price. OTM put: exercise price < current price. ATM options have: delta ≈ ±0.50, peak gamma, peak vega among same-expiry options, fastest absolute theta decay. ATM options are most actively traded because their Greeks are most sensitive to vol and time changes — making them the primary instruments for vol trading.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Automatic Exercise Thresholds and Do-Not-Exercise Notices
body: At expiration, exchanges automatically exercise any ITM option above a threshold: $0.05 for retail, $0.02 for professionals. Lower threshold for professionals because their per-trade transaction costs are lower — exercise profitable at smaller ITM amounts. A holder who does not want exercise must file a do-not-exercise notice. This creates pin risk for short-option holders: when stock is near the strike at expiration, the holder may or may not exercise, and the short party doesn't know if assignment will occur until after close. Pin risk is largest when the underlying is within $0.05–$0.10 of the strike.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Long Options Can Lose Even When Direction Is Correct
body: A critical principle: a long option position requires both correct direction AND sufficient speed of movement. If the underlying moves in the right direction but too slowly, time decay (theta) can exceed the value gained from the directional move, resulting in a net loss. This is the fundamental tradeoff of buying options vs. buying the underlying: options have capped risk but require the move to happen fast enough. The option buyer is paying for the right but also paying theta every day. Three-part forecast required: direction, magnitude, and timing. Getting one or two right while missing the third loses.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Theoretical Edge Is Necessary But Not Sufficient: Risk Also Matters
body: Determining theoretical value (expected value) is only half the problem. Because option values are probability-based, the laws of probability only guarantee outcomes in the long run. A single trade with positive edge can still lose. A trader must also consider: (1) the variance of outcomes — a wide distribution means a single trade may deviate far from expected value; (2) the required capital to weather adverse outcomes; (3) whether the edge is large enough relative to the variance to justify the risk. A small edge on a large, volatile position is not equivalent to a large edge on a small position.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Option Theoretical Value as Expected Value
body: The theoretical value of an option equals the expected value of its payoff at expiration, discounted to the present. If an option can expire worth $0, $2, $12, or $22 with probabilities 40%, 30%, 20%, 10%: E[payoff] = $0.60 + $2.40 + $2.20 = $5.20. The present value accounts for interest: if rates are 12%/year and expiration is 2 months, theoretical value = $5.20 / (1 + 0.12 × 2/12) = $5.10. A pricing model is a formalized, continuous version of this expected-value calculation using a probability distribution for the underlying at expiration. Black-Scholes uses the lognormal distribution.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Interest and Time Value: Why Options Require Discounting
body: Even if an option's expected payoff is known with certainty, its present value differs from its expected future value because of the time value of money. If a casino promises to pay $36 winnings two months from now rather than immediately, the present value of that $36 is less (e.g., $35.30 at 12% annual rate). Similarly, the theoretical value of an option is the present value of its expected payoff at expiration. For options with stock-type settlement, the option premium is paid upfront, so the full premium (not just intrinsic value) must be discounted. This is why options are worth more when interest rates are higher (for calls) — the cost of carry increases the forward price.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Pricing Models Are Tools, Not Truth: Using Them Correctly
body: Option pricing models are probability-based tools that help traders make better decisions, but they are not infallible. A trader who ignores models is flying blind. A trader paralyzed by model uncertainty (analysis paralysis) cannot profit either. The correct approach: use the model as a framework for thinking about option value, while maintaining full awareness of its assumptions and limitations. The most important limitation: all models require a volatility input that cannot be observed directly. A model's output is only as good as the volatility estimate used as input.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Probability Distribution Determines Option Value
body: The theoretical value of an option depends entirely on the probability distribution assumed for the underlying at expiration. The higher the volatility input, the wider the distribution, and the higher the expected value of OTM options. Different distribution assumptions (normal, lognormal, fat-tailed) produce different theoretical values for the same option. This is why traders argue about volatility: it is a disagreement about the shape and width of the distribution. Implied volatility is the distribution width implied by market prices — it is the market's consensus about how wide the distribution will be.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Eurodollar/Interest-Rate Options: Price Inversion
body: Interest-rate options are quoted on indexed prices (Eurodollar: 100 − interest rate). A 93.00 call in listed terms = a 7.00% put in interest-rate terms — they represent the same position. A correct model makes this transformation automatically. Failure to understand this inversion causes directional errors: buying a Eurodollar call when you expect rates to fall is correct (rates fall → price rises from 93 toward 100), but mistaking the contract as equivalent to a commodity call can lead to the wrong conclusion. Always verify the quoting convention before trading interest-rate derivatives.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Compounding Conventions: Simple, Periodic, Continuous
body: The future value of $1,000 at 12% annual rate after 1 year: (1) Simple interest: $1,120; (2) Monthly compounding: $1,126.83; (3) Continuous compounding: e^0.12 × $1,000 = $1,127.50. Black-Scholes uses continuous compounding. For option pricing, the compounding convention affects theoretical values and Greeks, especially rho and theta's interest-rate component. When comparing models or broker quotes, always confirm which convention is used. The difference is small for short-dated options but meaningful for LEAPS or multi-year positions.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Lognormal Distribution: Why Option Pricing Uses Log Returns
body: Stock prices are bounded below by zero but have unlimited upside, creating asymmetric (lognormal) price distributions. Logarithmic returns ln(P_t/P_{t-1}) are symmetrically normally distributed even though price levels are lognormally distributed. Black-Scholes exploits this: volatility = annualized standard deviation of log returns; future prices are lognormally distributed around the forward price. Consequences: (1) the probability of any upward move is calculated using the lognormal distribution, not the normal; (2) the mean of the lognormal distribution exceeds the current forward price (Jensen's inequality); (3) options on high-price stocks have higher dollar vega than equivalent options on low-price stocks.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: The IV-HV Gap: Investigating Market vs. Model Discrepancy
body: When a theoretical value is $2.94 but market trades at $3.40, IV exceeds the trader's forecast. This discrepancy has three possible explanations: (1) Structural demand: persistent hedging demand inflates option prices regardless of fair value; (2) Information asymmetry: the market knows something about upcoming events; (3) Wrong forecast: the trader's vol estimate is too low. The correct response: investigate before trading. Blindly selling IV because it seems high has been the source of many large losses when IV continues to rise. Always ask: why is IV where it is? before assuming mispricing.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Risk Measurement: The Fundamental Tradeoff Between Reward and Risk
body: Every market participant must balance reward and risk. A trader who focuses only on reward ignores the possibility of error. A trader who focuses only on risk cannot profit. The Greeks are the primary tools for measuring option risk: delta (directional risk), gamma (rate of delta change — curvature risk), theta (time risk), vega (volatility risk), rho (interest-rate risk). No position can have positive theoretical edge without accepting some form of Greek risk. Risk management means understanding which Greeks are large and ensuring no single Greek can cause an unacceptable loss.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Interest Rate Effects on Option Values: Calls vs. Puts
body: For stock options: increasing interest rates raises call values and lowers put values. Two effects: (1) Rising rates increase the forward price (cost of carry); (2) Rising rates reduce the present value of the option. For calls, the forward price increase dominates — calls rise. For puts, the forward price increase hurts (puts benefit from lower forward price), so puts fall. Deep ITM calls have the highest rho. For options on futures with futures-type settlement, interest rates have less effect because there is no cost of carry on the futures contract itself.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Dividends and Short Stock: Effect on Option Pricing
body: When a trader is short stock, the expected dividend reduces the forward price, lowering call values and raising put values. A short-stock holder therefore should: be willing to sell calls at a lower price (they're worth less) or buy puts at a higher price (they're worth more). This creates a natural hedge: selling calls or buying puts against short stock allows the trader to hedge the short back into a long position at the adjusted forward price. This is the mechanics behind conversion/reversal arbitrage in dividend-paying stocks.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Greeks as Instantaneous Partial Derivatives
body: The five standard Greeks are all partial derivatives of the option pricing function: delta = ∂V/∂S, gamma = ∂²V/∂S², theta = ∂V/∂t (time), vega = ∂V/∂σ, rho = ∂V/∂r. Each measures sensitivity while holding other variables constant. As partial derivatives, they are valid only for infinitesimally small changes — approximations for any finite move. For large moves: use delta + ½ × gamma × ΔS² for better accuracy. Greeks must be recalculated continuously as market conditions change — a snapshot from the morning is not valid after a significant price move.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Gamma: Delta's Rate of Change
body: Gamma = how much delta changes per one-point move in the underlying. All long options (calls and puts) have positive gamma. Rule: when underlying rises, add gamma to old delta; when underlying falls, subtract gamma from old delta. Example: call with delta 40, gamma 4, underlying at 97.50. If underlying rises to 101.50 (+4 points): average delta = (40 + 56)/2 = 48; new option value ≈ old value + 4 × 0.48. Long gamma means delta accelerates in your favor as the underlying moves. Short gamma means delta moves adversely. Gamma is the primary risk measure for dynamic hedgers.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Building Position Gamma from Individual Options
body: For a multi-option portfolio: position gamma is additive. Total position gamma = Σ(individual gamma × contract quantity × 100). Long options add positive gamma; short options add negative gamma. A trader with large positive gamma wants the underlying to move — in either direction — because each move creates a scalp profit. A trader with large negative gamma dreads large moves — each move creates an accelerating loss. The net gamma of the entire book is the most important single risk number for a market maker to monitor.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Delta Is an Approximation: Gamma Matters for Large Moves
body: Delta gives the rate of change of option value for a small move. For large moves, delta-only estimates are increasingly inaccurate because delta itself changes (gamma). Better approximation: ΔV ≈ delta × ΔS + ½ × gamma × ΔS². For a short-gamma position, this second term is negative — losses are larger than delta alone predicts. Example: short a straddle, delta = 0 but gamma = −20. A 5-point move causes delta-estimated loss of 0, but actual loss ≈ ½ × 20 × 25 = 250 points. Always consider gamma when estimating P/L for large underlying moves.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Theoretical Edge and the Casino Analogy
body: A position with positive theoretical edge means, on average and over many repetitions, the trader should profit by the amount of the edge. Like a casino: the house edge is small per game but reliable across millions of games. Options trading works the same way: selling options at above theoretical value, or buying at below theoretical value, creates positive edge. But edge only manifests in the long run — any single trade can lose. A trader needs: (1) a positive edge per trade; (2) sufficient size to make edge statistically meaningful; (3) capital to weather variance from expected value.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Using Greeks to Characterize a Position's Risk Profile
body: Delta and gamma together describe the directional characteristics of a position: delta tells you which direction helps; gamma tells you how fast you want the market to move. A position with +delta and +gamma: benefits from upward moves that accelerate. A position with +delta and −gamma: benefits from slow, steady upward moves — fast moves hurt. Theta and vega describe the time and volatility characteristics. A full risk profile requires knowing the signs and magnitudes of all four main Greeks simultaneously. Managing a position means keeping these Greeks within acceptable bounds.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Exploiting Underpriced Options: Long Delta-Neutral Hedge
body: When an option is below theoretical value (market price < theoretical price), buy the option and delta-hedge with the underlying. Example: June 100 call has theoretical value 5.89, market offers at 5.00. Buy the calls, short the delta in underlying to neutralize direction. Theoretical edge = 5.89 − 5.00 = 0.89 per contract. The position profits when realized volatility exceeds the IV implied by the market price of 5.00. This edge is earned through gamma scalps over the holding period. Risk: the actual realized vol may fall short of the IV implied by theoretical value.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Delta-Neutral Adjustments: Rebalancing to Maintain Hedge
body: After initiating a delta-neutral hedge (buying options + shorting underlying), the delta drifts as the underlying moves (due to gamma). To restore neutrality: if the underlying rises and delta becomes positive, sell more underlying; if the underlying falls and delta becomes negative, buy more underlying. These rebalancing trades are adjustments — they don't affect theoretical edge because the underlying has no theoretical value in an options framework. The cumulative profit from all adjustment trades is the gamma scalp P/L. Total position P/L = theoretical edge at initiation + gamma scalp P/L + theta paid + vega P/L.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Closing a Delta-Neutral Position at Expiration
body: At expiration of a delta-neutral position, closure procedure: (1) Let OTM options expire worthless; (2) Sell ITM options at parity (intrinsic value) or exercise and offset in the underlying; (3) Liquidate any outstanding underlying contracts at market. This systematic closure locks in all P/L. The final realized P/L = sum of all gamma scalps throughout the holding period, minus theta paid, plus/minus vega P/L from IV changes, plus/minus interest on underlying position. P&L attribution to each component is essential for evaluating whether the strategy worked as intended.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Interest on Underlying Hedge Position
body: A delta-neutral hedge shorting 50 underlying at 97.70 generates $4,885 in proceeds earning 6% × 70/365 = $56.21 interest over the holding period. Each rebalancing trade also generates a cash credit or debit that earns or costs interest until expiration. This interest component is part of the true P/L — often small at low interest rates but significant at high rates. The full theoretical value of the option accounts for this cost of carry. Traders who ignore interest when computing actual P/L will overstate or understate results.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Repeated Hedging: Why Edge Requires Many Repetitions
body: A single delta-neutral hedge with positive theoretical edge can still lose — the laws of probability only guarantee results in the long run. The adjustment process (gamma scalping) forces the trader to make many small bets at the same favorable odds, spreading variance across many trades. A trader who rebalances frequently will have a P/L closer to the theoretical expectation than one who rebalances rarely. The analogy: a casino game with 0.5% house edge on a single $1,000 bet is risky; the same edge spread across 10,000 $0.10 bets is nearly certain to profit.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Gamma Curvature: Why Long Gamma Always Profits from Large Moves
body: The curvature of an option's value curve (positive gamma for long options) creates a mathematical asymmetry: for a given price change ΔS, the long-gamma position gains more from favorable moves than it loses from unfavorable moves of equal magnitude. This is because delta itself shifts in the favorable direction as the underlying moves. The aggregate of all delta-neutral rebalancing trades (buy on dips, sell on rallies) is always positive for a long-gamma position, regardless of direction. The cost of this free asymmetry is theta — the daily decay of time value.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Breakeven Volatility: When Gamma Profits Equal Theta Cost
body: A long-gamma, delta-neutral position has a breakeven realized volatility. If realized vol exceeds this breakeven, gamma scalps > theta paid → profit. If realized vol falls short, theta paid > gamma scalps → loss. The breakeven vol is closely related to the implied volatility at which the options were purchased — if you buy at 30% IV, breakeven realized vol is approximately 30%. The more the underlying moves (higher realized vol), the more each rebalancing trade captures. In an extremely quiet market, gamma scalps are negligible and theta eats the position.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Theta Acceleration: ATM Options Decay Fastest Near Expiry
body: Theta of ATM options accelerates as expiration approaches — the daily decay rate approaches infinity at the final moment. For ITM and OTM options, theta actually slows near expiry (they have less time premium to decay). The practical implication: an ATM option with 1 week remaining decays faster per day than the same option with 1 month remaining. The theta-gamma tradeoff is most extreme near expiry for ATM options: maximum daily income (theta) but maximum gamma risk simultaneously. Calendar spread traders who are short near-term ATM options benefit most from this acceleration.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Theta Proportional to Volatility for ATM Options
body: For ATM options, theta is essentially directly proportional to volatility. If IV doubles, theta approximately doubles. This makes intuitive sense: higher vol means more time premium, which decays faster in absolute dollar terms. The graph of ATM option value vs. time is approximately linear, with theta being the slope. For an ATM option with 26% IV, the daily theta is approximately proportional to vol/√252 × underlying price × delta. This proportionality is useful for quickly estimating theta changes when IV changes — if IV rises 10%, expect ATM theta to increase ~10%.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Vega Is Constant for ATM Options Across Volatility Levels
body: An ATM option's value vs. implied volatility graph is approximately linear. Because vega is the slope of this graph, the vega of an ATM option is relatively constant across different volatility levels (20%, 30%, 40%). This means: for ATM options, a 1% increase in IV always produces approximately the same dollar change in value regardless of where IV starts. For OTM and ITM options, vega is not constant — the value vs. IV graph is curved, meaning vega itself changes with volatility (volga).

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Volga (Vomma): Sensitivity of Vega to Volatility
body: Volga (also called vomma or dvega/dvol) = the rate of change of vega with respect to implied volatility. For ATM options, volga ≈ 0 (vega is nearly constant). For OTM and ITM options, volga is positive — vega increases as vol increases. Volga is maximum for options with deltas around 10 and 90 (deep OTM/ITM). As time increases, volga for OTM/ITM options becomes more sensitive to vol level. Practical implication: OTM options have significant volga — their vega increases as IV rises, creating convex vol exposure. Long volga positions profit if vol rises significantly (vol-of-vol bets).

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Higher-Order Greeks: Greeks of the Greeks
body: Beyond the five standard Greeks, higher-order Greeks measure how the primary Greeks change: (1) Gamma = how delta changes with price; (2) Vanna = how delta changes with vol (= how vega changes with price); (3) Volga/vomma = how vega changes with vol; (4) Charm = how delta changes with time (delta decay); (5) Speed = how gamma changes with price; (6) Veta = how vega changes with time. These second-order Greeks matter for managing large positions over time or in volatile markets. A position with extreme vanna, for example, will see its delta hedges become unbalanced if vol moves significantly.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Volatility's Effect on Delta: High Vol Pulls All Deltas Toward 50
body: In a high-volatility environment: OTM options have higher deltas (closer to 50) because there is more probability they expire ITM; ITM options have lower deltas (also closer to 50) because there is more probability they expire OTM. In a low-volatility environment: OTM options have lower deltas (closer to 0); ITM options have higher deltas (closer to 1 or -1). The practical implication: OTM options bought at low vol will see their deltas rise significantly if vol spikes. Conversely, ITM options become more ATM-like at high vol, making them useful for delta-hedging strategies.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Time and Volatility Have Parallel Effects on Option Value
body: More time to expiration acts similarly to higher volatility: both increase the likelihood of large price changes and raise option values. Conversely, less time is like lower volatility. This parallel means that strategies designed to profit from time decay (short theta) often also require tolerance for low volatility (short vega). Traders can sometimes substitute one dimension for the other when constructing positions — a calendar spread exploits this: the near-term option has less effective 'vol-time' than the far-term option.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Why Spreads: Four Reasons Traders Use Them
body: Option spreads serve four distinct purposes: (1) Relative value — when absolute IV is uncertain but one option appears mispriced vs. another, spread the two to capture relative mispricing; (2) Directional with a specific scenario — construct a position that profits specifically within a forecast range; (3) Reducing variance — spreading reduces the variance of outcomes compared to outright positions, making edge more reliable in the short run; (4) Capital efficiency — many spreads require less margin than outright positions for similar exposure. Most professional options trading involves spreads rather than outright positions.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Spreads Increase Breakeven Volatility Range (Margin for Error)
body: A key advantage of spreading: it increases the range of outcomes over which the position is profitable. An outright short straddle at 25% IV breaks even only if realized vol stays near 25%. A spread against the straddle might allow profitability for realized vols between 20% and 35% — a much wider range. This wider breakeven range means more occurrences when the trader is right. Spreads trade potential maximum profit for reliability of profit. For traders with positive-edge strategies, reliability is more valuable than maximum profit.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Straddle: Long ATM Call + Long ATM Put
body: A long straddle consists of a long ATM call and a long ATM put with the same strike and expiration. Greek characteristics: +gamma (profits from large moves in either direction), −theta (pays daily), +vega (profits from rising IV). The straddle profits when: realized vol > implied vol (large moves from gamma scalps), or IV rises (vega gain). The straddle loses when: underlying is quiet and IV falls. At expiration, the straddle breaks even when the underlying is at the strike ± (call premium + put premium). A short straddle has the inverse profile: collects premium, profits from quiet/declining vol.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Strangle: OTM Call + OTM Put Spread
body: A long strangle consists of a long OTM call and a long OTM put with different strikes (both out-of-the-money) at the same expiration. Greek profile: +gamma, −theta, +vega — identical in sign to a straddle. Differences from straddle: lower cost (both legs OTM), wider breakeven range at expiration, lower gamma and vega per dollar invested. A guts strangle uses ITM options instead of OTM options — equivalent P/L but different pricing due to intrinsic value. In practice, OTM strangles are more actively traded than ITM strangles because they require less capital and have lower absolute vega risk.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Butterfly Spread: Structure and Payoff
body: A long call butterfly: +1 lower call / −2 middle call / +1 upper call. Maximum profit at expiration: when underlying is at the body (middle strike). Maximum value = spread width − premium paid. Example: 90/100/110 call butterfly. If underlying at 100: 90 call worth $10, 100 and 110 calls worth $0, position worth $10. Below 90 or above 110: worth $0. The butterfly pays maximum when the underlying is exactly at the body, and zero when it's outside the wings. This is the opposite of a straddle: profits from a quiet, range-bound market.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Size vs. Risk: Butterflies Can Be Larger Positions with Less Risk
body: In options, size and risk do not always correlate. A trader can buy 300 butterflies (300 × 600 × 300) with less total risk than selling 100 straddles. Why: the butterfly has defined, limited risk (premium paid) with a large potential reward if the underlying pins near the body. The straddle has large gamma and vega risk that can create substantial losses if the market moves far. This counterintuitive relationship — where larger size has lower risk — is a fundamental property of spread positions. Managing risk by structure is often more important than managing risk by position size alone.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Calendar Spread: Why It Benefits from Time Passage and Rising IV
body: A long calendar spread (short near-term, long far-term, same strike) increases in value when: (1) Time passes with underlying near the strike — the near-term option decays faster (ATM theta accelerates near expiry) while the far-term option decays more slowly; (2) IV rises — the far-term option has higher vega (more time), so the long side benefits more than the short side loses. The calendar spread loses value when: the underlying moves far from the strike (both options become OTM or ITM, reducing time premium difference), or IV falls.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Calendar Spread Time Value Increase: Theta Differential
body: The calendar spread value increases as time passes because of ATM theta acceleration: the near-term option (which is short) decays faster per day than the far-term option (which is long). This theta differential is the calendar spread's 'rent.' As expiration of the near-term option approaches, its theta accelerates dramatically for ATM options, while the far-term option's theta is relatively stable. The maximum value of the calendar spread typically occurs near the expiration of the short-term option, when both options are still ATM.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Pre-Event IV Rise: Quiet Stock, Rising Options
body: Before a significant known event (earnings, FDA, central bank), the underlying stock may remain quiet while IV rises. Traders price in the anticipated large post-event move. Conditions: (1) low realized vol pre-event (gamma scalps negligible); (2) rising IV pre-event (positive vega). Long calendar spreads or long vega positions benefit pre-event because the far-term option has more vega exposure. After the event, vol crush typically occurs — IV collapses even if the stock makes a large move. Short calendar spreads (short vega) can benefit post-event.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Vertical Spread Payoff: Bounded Between 0 and Spread Width
body: A vertical spread (long lower strike / short upper strike call, or long upper / short lower put) always expires between 0 and the spread width. A 100/105 call vertical: expires at $0 if underlying < 100, at $5 if underlying > 105. A 95/105 put vertical: worth $0 if market > 105, $10 if market < 95. The bounded payoff defines maximum profit and maximum loss — both are known at entry. Trading range: always within [0, spread width]. This makes verticals ideal for expressing directional views with defined risk.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Selecting the Best Vertical Spread
body: Given many available strikes and expiries, criteria for optimal vertical spread: (1) Strike selection — use the current underlying price as the body; choose width based on your price target range. (2) Expiry selection — match holding period to anticipated timeline for the move. (3) IV comparison — check that the short leg has higher IV than the long leg (sell high IV, buy low IV relative to skew). (4) Risk-reward — wider spreads collect more premium in credit spreads but require more space for the underlying to move. The ideal spread maximizes (edge per dollar risked) × (probability of profit).

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Condor: Four-Legged Wider Butterfly
body: A condor consists of four legs: +1 lowest call / −1 lower-middle call / −1 upper-middle call / +1 highest call (or puts equivalently). The condor's maximum profit range is wider than a butterfly (between the two inner strikes instead of only at one strike). The condor pays maximum when the underlying is between the two short strikes at expiration. Call condor and put condor of the same strikes have identical characteristics (put-call parity). Condors are preferred over butterflies when a wider profit zone is desired but maximum profit is lower per dollar of risk.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Ratio Spreads: Asymmetric Payoff with Credit Potential
body: A call ratio spread: long fewer lower-strike calls, short more upper-strike calls (e.g., +1 call / −2 higher calls). Credit received upfront. P/L: profits if the underlying stays below the short strike; limited profit if underlying moves above the long strike; large losses if underlying moves far above the short strikes (naked short call exposure). Put ratio spreads are equivalent with puts. Ratio spreads are typically initiated for a credit — they profit from quiet to moderately bullish/bearish markets but have uncapped risk on one side. Requires strict stop-loss management.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Vertical Spread Mid-Life Value: Probability Driven
body: Before expiration, a vertical spread's value reflects the probability of the underlying finishing above or below the strikes. If underlying is at 80 and strikes are 100/105: call spread ≈ $0 (unlikely to reach strikes); put spread ≈ $10 (very likely to finish below 95). If underlying is at 120: call spread ≈ $5; put spread ≈ $0. Between strikes, value is intermediate. This probability-based valuation means: as the underlying approaches the spread range, the credit spread's risk increases rapidly. Managing credit spreads requires monitoring the underlying's proximity to the short strike.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Margin for Error in Spreads: Context-Dependent
body: What constitutes an adequate margin for error in a spread depends on the volatility characteristics of the specific market. A 5 percentage point vol margin may be extremely tight in a high-vol market where vol swings 10+ points routinely, but ample in a stable market. Traders must calibrate their required margin for error to the historical range of vol in their specific market. A margin for error that seems comfortable based on average conditions may be dangerously tight during a vol spike. Always stress-test your vol assumption: what happens if your forecast is wrong by 50%?

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Spread Adjustments: When to Adjust and How
body: Two types of adjustments in spread trading: (1) Delta adjustments — rebalancing when delta drifts too far from neutral; (2) Greek adjustments — changing the spread's Greek profile (gamma, vega, theta) when the position's risk characteristics become unacceptable. Methods for delta adjustment: sell underlying, sell calls, or buy puts. The best adjustment method: whichever improves the risk-reward characteristics of the overall position most efficiently. Avoid adjustments that increase gamma or vega risk beyond acceptable levels. Each adjustment should improve the position's theoretical edge or reduce risk.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Adjustment Methods: Underlying vs. Options
body: When a spread needs a delta adjustment and the underlying is available, the choice between adjusting with underlying vs. options has significant implications: Underlying adjustments: (1) no change to gamma/vega; (2) direct, clean delta change; (3) adds interest cost on the underlying position. Option adjustments: (1) change both delta and gamma/vega; (2) may create theoretical edge on the adjustment trade itself; (3) can improve or worsen the spread's risk profile. Traders who can capture edge on adjustment trades (buying underpriced, selling overpriced options) prefer option adjustments. When no edge is available, underlying adjustments are simpler.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Reducing Position Size When Risk Is Too High
body: A disciplined trader knows that sometimes, because of risk considerations, reducing position size — even at a cost (giving up theoretical edge) — is the right action. If a spread has moved against the trader and risk parameters are being breached, reducing size is more important than maintaining maximum theoretical edge. Risk control is always the primary concern. Traders who refuse to reduce size when risk parameters are exceeded typically suffer larger losses later. Rule: define maximum acceptable risk before entry; reduce size (not just adjust) when that risk is breached.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Synthetic Positions from Put-Call Parity: Full Table
body: Put-call parity: C − P = F − K × e^(−rT) (for European options on futures). From this, all six synthetic positions: (1) Synthetic long underlying = long call + short put (same strike); (2) Synthetic short underlying = short call + long put; (3) Synthetic long call = long underlying + long put; (4) Synthetic short call = short underlying + short put; (5) Synthetic long put = short underlying + long call; (6) Synthetic short put = long underlying + short call (= covered call). All have identical risk to the real position. Covered call = synthetic short put — same downside, same risk.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Call Delta + Put Delta = 100 (Absolute Values)
body: For a call and put with the same exercise price and expiration: |delta_call| + |delta_put| ≈ 100. If the 100 put has delta −60, the 100 call has delta +40. This relationship holds approximately because a synthetic long (long call + short put) replicates long stock (delta = +100). Precise equality would require delta_call − delta_put = 1 (for stock-type settlement) or adjustments for futures-type settlement. This relationship is useful for: quickly computing the call delta from the put delta, verifying consistency in option chains, and constructing delta-neutral positions.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Six Synthetic Equivalences Applied to Spreads
body: Every option spread can be rewritten using synthetics. A bull call spread (+lower call / −upper call) = −(bear put spread) = long call spread at same strikes. A long straddle (long call + long put) = long underlying + 2 long puts = short underlying + 2 long calls. A long butterfly (+lower / −2 middle / +upper) can be expressed as a long call spread + short call spread. Understanding these equivalences lets traders: (1) find cheaper construction paths using skew; (2) verify P/L calculations; (3) identify equivalent positions for margin purposes.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Time Box: Diagonal Spread Intermonth Arbitrage
body: A time box = two diagonal spreads: +1 near-month lower call / −1 far-month upper call / −1 near-month lower put / +1 far-month upper put. The time box exploits mispricings in the volatility term structure — if August IV is too high relative to June IV, the time box generates a credit exceeding fair value. Unlike a regular box spread (which arbitrages put-call parity at one expiration), a time box arbitrages the volatility relationship between two expirations. Used primarily by market makers monitoring term-structure mispricings.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: American Call Early Exercise: Pseudo-American Valuation
body: American calls on dividend-paying stocks may be worth exercising early — just before the ex-dividend date. The pseudo-American method: calculate the call value assuming: (1) expiration the day before ex-dividend (call worth its intrinsic + remaining time value), vs. (2) normal expiration with underlying price reduced by expected dividend. Take the higher value. If the dividend exceeds the remaining time value, early exercise is optimal. Traders holding short ITM calls on dividend-paying stocks must monitor this: assignment risk increases sharply when the dividend exceeds the option's time premium.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Barone-Adesi/Whaley: Faster American Option Pricing
body: The Cox-Ross-Rubinstein binomial model prices American options accurately but is computationally slow (many lattice steps). Barone-Adesi and Whaley (1987) introduced a quadratic approximation that runs significantly faster while maintaining good accuracy. Used widely for real-time American option pricing and risk management. The BAW model is particularly accurate for equity options where early exercise is driven primarily by dividends (calls) or interest rates (puts). Less accurate for very long-dated options where the quadratic approximation breaks down.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: American Put Premium: Largest in Low-Vol, High-Rate Environments
body: The American put's excess value over its European counterpart (early exercise premium) is largest when: (1) Volatility is low — the put is more likely to stay deep ITM; waiting adds little additional value from future movement; (2) Interest rates are high — the time value of collecting intrinsic value today exceeds the optionality of waiting. The premium shrinks at high volatility because large future moves make waiting more valuable. Practical implication: deep ITM puts should be analyzed for early exercise when vol is low and rates are high. The risk for short-put holders: unexpected early assignment.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Collar: Combining Put Protection with Call Premium
body: A collar on a long stock position: buy OTM put (protection) + sell OTM call (premium offset). Example: stock at 100, buy 95 put, sell 105 call. Protected below 95; profit capped above 105. A zero-cost collar sets strikes so premium received = premium paid. Collar = long stock + long put + short call = long stock + synthetic short stock risk reversal. Equivalent to a vertical spread on the underlying. Used by institutional investors to cheaply hedge concentrated equity positions. The tradeoff: upside is capped in exchange for downside protection.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Volatility-Aware Hedging Beyond Simple Puts
body: Simple hedges (buying a put, selling a covered call) are most common but not optimal in all situations. More sophisticated alternatives: (1) Ratio put spreads — buy more lower puts, sell fewer higher puts, for net debit or credit; cheaper than outright puts but limited protection; (2) Calendar spreads — short near-term option to finance far-term protection; (3) Delta-neutral overlays — systematically hedge directional risk dynamically. Each approach involves a different tradeoff between protection cost, upside participation, and complexity.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Hedger's Three-Question Framework
body: Before constructing a hedge, answer: (1) Is this disaster insurance (must protect at worst case)? → only buying options qualifies; choice is which strike. (2) How much directional risk to eliminate? → determines option strike (ATM = full hedge, OTM = partial hedge) and position size. (3) What additional risks are acceptable? → determines whether to sell an option to finance the hedge (collar, ratio spread) or accept the cost of a pure long option. Most hedge failures come from not answering question 3 explicitly — traders inadvertently accept risks they didn't intend to take (e.g., a short call in a collar capping a large recovery).

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Black-Scholes Delta: N(d1) and Normal Distribution
body: In Black-Scholes, call delta = N(d₁) = cumulative standard normal at d₁. For an option with 1% vol (1/100 of a standard deviation), the peak of the standard normal is ≈ 0.399/100 = 0.00399 per delta unit. Delta ranges 0→1 for calls and 0→−1 for puts. ATM call delta ≈ 0.50 (not exactly, due to forward price adjustment). For European options: the call delta also approximates the risk-neutral probability of expiring ITM. This interpretation is useful: a 30-delta option has approximately a 30% probability of expiring in-the-money under the risk-neutral measure.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Theta Components: Volatility Decay vs. Interest Effects
body: Black-Scholes theta has two components: (1) Volatility value decay — always negative for long options; equal in sign for calls and puts; dominates in most conditions; (2) Interest-rate components — can be positive or negative depending on settlement type and whether call or put. For deep ITM calls, the interest component (cost of carry benefit) partially offsets decay. For deep ITM puts, interest adds to decay (waiting costs you the interest you could earn). Total theta = sum of both components. In most practical situations, the decay component dominates and theta is simply the daily time value erosion.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Vega Decreases with Time for Some Stock Options
body: Increasing time to expiration raises vega for most options, but not all. For stock options, the forward price = S × e^(rT). As time increases, the forward price rises (positive interest rates), which can move the option away from ATM. Since ATM options have maximum vega, becoming less ATM reduces vega. A deep ITM stock call may have lower vega for longer expiries than shorter ones — counterintuitive. This matters for: LEAPS pricing, long-dated collar analysis, and any strategy where the vega assumption is 'longer = higher vega.' Always verify using a pricing model rather than assuming.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Historical Volatility: Standard Deviation of Log Returns
body: Calculation: (1) Compute log returns: r_i = ln(P_i / P_{i-1}); (2) Find mean: r̄ = (1/n) × Σr_i; (3) Compute sample std dev: σ_daily = √[Σ(r_i − r̄)² / (n−1)]; (4) Annualize: σ_annual = σ_daily × √252. Using (n−1) divisor gives unbiased estimate. Log returns are preferred over percentage returns because: they are additive over time, symmetric for equal up/down moves, and naturally bounded (avoiding negative prices). Daily settlement-to-settlement returns are standard for exchange-traded options. Increasing the lookback N improves stability but reduces responsiveness to recent vol changes.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Lookback Window Choice in HV Calculation
body: The lookback period for historical volatility represents a tradeoff: (1) Short window (20 days): responsive to recent vol changes, noisy; (2) Medium window (60 days): balanced; (3) Long window (252 days): stable, slow to react to vol regime changes. Most practitioners compare multiple lookbacks simultaneously: 20-day vs. 60-day vs. 252-day HV. When short-term HV > long-term HV, vol is elevated (backwardation-like); when short < long, vol is below its long-run average (normal conditions). The comparison informs whether current IV is elevated or depressed relative to recent realized vol.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Parkinson and Garman-Klass: High-Low Volatility Estimators
body: Two efficiency-improving HV estimators using intraday data: (1) Parkinson (1980): uses daily high and low prices; requires fewer data points to achieve same accuracy as close-to-close. Formula uses the squared range: σ² ∝ Σ(ln(H/L))². (2) Garman-Klass (1980): uses open, high, low, close; further improves efficiency. Both produce consistently lower volatility estimates than close-to-close because they exclude overnight gaps. Applicable only during continuous trading hours. For assets with significant overnight price gaps (earnings, gaps on news), these estimators understate true volatility. Use close-to-close for assets with frequent gaps.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: IV Term Structure: Identifying Overpriced and Underpriced Months
body: The implied volatility term structure plots IV against expiration date for a fixed strike. A smooth term structure (fitted curve) represents 'fair' calendar spread pricing. Months that plot above the smooth curve are relatively overpriced; months below are underpriced. Calendar spreads between an overpriced near month and a fairly-priced far month generate a premium vs. fair value. The term structure in backwardation (near > far) typically occurs during high-vol, high-fear environments; normal contango (near < far) reflects the baseline uncertainty premium for future time periods.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Forward Volatility: Calculating IV Between Two Dates
body: Forward vol for the period t₁ → t₂ given term structure: σ_forward = √[(σ₂² × t₂ − σ₁² × t₁) / (t₂ − t₁)]. This is the break-even realized vol implied by a calendar spread between t₁ and t₂. If the actual calendar spread trades below this forward vol, the spread is cheap; if above, it is expensive. Example: 30-day IV = 25%, 60-day IV = 22%. Forward vol for days 30-60 = √[(0.22² × 60 − 0.25² × 30) / 30] = √[0.03... ] ≈ 18.7%. A calendar spread at 18% IV is cheap vs. this forward.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Market Maker Pricing: Three-Question Framework
body: A market maker prices options using three sequential questions: (1) What does the marketplace think the option is worth? (current market mid-price → market IV); (2) What do I think it's worth? (my theoretical value from my vol forecast); (3) What positions am I carrying? (inventory). If I think value > market: I want to buy → bid below my theoretical value to capture edge. If I already hold too many long options: shade the bid lower to avoid adding more. These three questions determine both the level of bid/ask and the width of the spread. Market makers are not predicting direction — they are capturing edge in a vol view vs. market IV.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Market Maker vs. Speculator: Different Risk Tolerances
body: Market makers and speculators operate with fundamentally different time horizons and risk tolerances. Market makers: goal is to capture bid-ask spread; hold positions for minutes to hours; delta-hedge immediately; care most about gamma and vega risk accumulating in the book. Speculators: hold for days to weeks; accept directional and vol risk; profit from forecasting ability. A market maker who fails to hedge promptly becomes an unintentional speculator — exposed to large adverse moves without the edge to justify the risk. The discipline of immediate hedging is non-negotiable for market makers.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Total-Return vs. Price-Return Index Options
body: Two main types of stock indexes: (1) Price-weighted (e.g., DJIA): divisor adjusts for dividends to prevent artificial index drops; dividends affect the forward price calculation for options; (2) Total-return: dividends reinvested — no price decline on ex-dividend date; forward price grows at risk-free rate alone. Options on a total-return index require no dividend adjustment in pricing models. Options on a price-weighted index require careful modeling of the dividend flow. Most equity index options (SPX, NDX) are on price-return indexes — dividends must be modeled.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Price-Weighted Index: Component Impact via Divisor
body: For a price-weighted index, change in index per $1 move in any component = $1 / divisor. Example: divisor = 1.50, then each $1 change in any component stock changes the index by $0.667, regardless of that stock's price. Higher-priced components dominate index moves in price-weighted indexes (unlike cap-weighted indexes where higher market-cap stocks dominate). Index option delta calculations must account for component weighting — the delta of an index option vs. a specific component stock is scaled by the component's weight in the index.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Trading Halted Components: Index Estimation
body: When a component stock is halted pending news, index traders estimate the stock's contribution using the midpoint of the price indication (e.g., midpoint of $67.50–$68.00 indication = $67.75) scaled by the stock's index weight. Index futures may trade based on this estimated index value. When the stock resumes trading, the index reprices, potentially creating a rapid adjustment in futures. Traders holding index positions when a component is halted carry the risk that the true reopening price differs from the estimate. This is a form of gap risk inherent in index products.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: The Six Black-Scholes Assumptions and Reality
body: Black-Scholes assumes: (1) Frictionless markets — no transaction costs, taxes, or borrowing restrictions; (2) Continuous trading — positions adjustable at any time; (3) Constant interest rates; (4) Constant volatility; (5) Volatility independent of underlying price; (6) Small price changes are normally distributed → lognormal prices at expiration. All six are violated in real markets. The most critical violations: (4) volatility is not constant (vol smile/skew); (6) fat tails and jumps create non-lognormal distributions. Practitioners use the model while managing the residual risk from these violations.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Margin Calls: Black-Scholes Frictionless Assumption Fails
body: Black-Scholes assumes unlimited frictionless borrowing and lending. In practice, margin calls can force position liquidation at the worst time — when a position is deeply against the trader. If additional capital is unavailable, the model's theoretical hedge cannot be maintained. This creates forced selling into adverse markets, amplifying losses. The practical implication: strategy capital requirements must account for worst-case margin demands, not just initial margin. Deep OTM short options that appear safe based on delta may require substantial additional margin if vol spikes and the underlying moves toward the strike.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Transaction Costs Erode Theoretical Edge
body: Black-Scholes assumes zero transaction costs. In practice, every gamma-neutral rebalancing trade incurs commissions and bid-ask spread costs. For high-gamma strategies requiring frequent adjustments, these costs can eliminate or reverse the theoretical edge. The number of rebalancing trades multiplied by cost per trade = total friction cost. Strategies that require 20+ adjustments per week at $2/contract each may pay $40+ per contract in friction alone — exceeding the initial theoretical edge. Retail traders with high per-trade costs must use much larger edges than market makers to achieve profitability net of transaction costs.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Volatility Smile: IV Differs Across Exercise Prices
body: In practice, implied volatility is not constant across strikes for the same expiration — it forms the 'volatility smile' or 'volatility skew.' Black-Scholes assumes constant IV, but market prices reveal that IV varies systematically with strike. The shape is observable by back-solving IV from market prices at each strike. For equity options, the smile is actually a skew (monotonically downward sloping), not symmetric. For FX options, the smile is often symmetric. For commodities, skew can be upward-sloping (upside skew) reflecting supply-shock risk.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Equity Skew: Two Forces Creating Persistent OTM Put Premium
body: Equity OTM puts have persistently higher IV than OTM calls (downward-sloping skew). Two simultaneous structural forces: (1) Insurance demand — investors continuously buy OTM puts for crash protection, creating buying pressure that inflates OTM put IV; (2) Covered call writing — investors owning stock systematically sell OTM calls to generate income, creating selling pressure that deflates OTM call IV. Both forces reinforce the skew: OTM puts bid up, OTM calls sold down. This structural premium makes selling OTM puts theoretically profitable on average — but with crash risk that materializes periodically.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Volatility Derivatives: Pure Exposure to Volatility as an Asset
body: Before VIX futures and variance swaps, no instrument allowed pure vol exposure without delta risk. Volatility derivatives: (1) VIX futures — trade on the expected 30-day IV of the S&P 500 30 days forward; typically in contango (futures > current VIX) due to uncertainty premium; (2) Variance swaps — pay realized variance minus fixed variance strike; mathematically simpler (variance is additive); (3) Volatility swaps — pay realized vol minus fixed vol; harder to replicate. These instruments allow: hedging vega without changing delta; speculating on vol-of-vol; expressing term structure views without legging into calendar spreads.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Realized Volatility Contract Settlement
body: A realized vol contract settles at the annualized standard deviation of log returns over its life. Returns use daily settlement prices. Annualization factor = √(trading days per year). At settlement, realized vol is unambiguous — no model, no IV, just the actual measured volatility. Variance contracts (pay realized variance − strike) are more common than volatility contracts because variance is additive: total variance over two periods = sum of period variances. Volatility is not additive. This additivity makes variance swaps easier to replicate with a static portfolio of options (the log-contract replication).

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Skew Shape Varies Significantly by Asset Class
body: Skew shape reflects asset-specific risk characteristics: (1) Equity indexes: steep downward skew — OTM puts >> OTM calls; crash risk is dominant fear; (2) Individual stocks: similar but less steep than indexes; idiosyncratic upside (M&A, earnings) reduces the extreme downward skew; (3) Commodities: often upward skew (OTM calls > OTM puts) for agricultural commodities — supply disruption risk is to the upside; mixed for energy; (4) Currencies: symmetric smile — crash risk is bidirectional; both OTM puts and calls elevated. Traders who apply equity skew intuitions to commodity or FX markets will systematically misprice options in those markets.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Risk Reversal: Synthetic Long/Short Underlying via Options
body: A risk reversal consists of a long call and short put (or vice versa) with the same underlying, expiration, but different strikes. A synthetic long underlying uses the same strike (equivalent to long stock). An actual risk reversal uses different strikes — creating net long or net short directional exposure with a specific skew structure. Long risk reversal (long call, short lower put): bullish with limited downside protection. Short risk reversal (short call, long lower put): bearish, equivalent to buying insurance. Risk reversals are used to express skew views: if you think OTM puts are overpriced relative to OTM calls, sell the put and buy the call — a short risk reversal collecting the skew premium.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Tau (τ): Time to Expiration in Option Formulas
body: Tau (τ) is standard notation for time to expiration in years. For 30 calendar days: τ = 30/365 ≈ 0.082. For 63 trading days: τ = 63/252 = 0.25. Tau appears throughout Black-Scholes: in the forward price, in d₁ and d₂, and in all Greeks. √τ scales volatility to the holding period: 30-day vol = annual vol × √(30/252). Practitioners must confirm the day-count convention used (365 calendar days vs. 252 trading days) — the two conventions produce different tau values and slightly different Greeks. For options with less than a week to expiry, the correct day count convention matters significantly for theta calculations.

author: Sheldon Natenberg
title: Vol-of-Vol: Risk in Long Vega Positions
body: Long vega positions (long options, long straddles) profit if IV rises. But IV itself is volatile — it can spike and crash unpredictably. The risk of a long vega position is not just from realized vol failing to meet IV; it also includes the risk that IV falls before the position is closed. This vol-of-vol risk is captured by volga (second derivative of option value to vol). Deep OTM options have high volga — their vega increases significantly if vol rises. In stressed markets, IV can mean-revert quickly after a spike, turning a profitable long-vega position negative within days. Long vol positions require active management of IV exposure.
